# Instructions

Manage robot factory settings.

When a robot comes off the factory floor, it has no name.

The first time you turn on a robot, a random name is generated in the format of two uppercase letters followed by three digits, such as RX837 or BC811.

Every once in a while we need to reset a robot to its factory settings, which means that its name gets wiped.
The next time you ask, that robot will respond with a new random name.

The names must be random: they should not follow a predictable sequence.
Using random names means a risk of collisions.
Your solution must ensure that every existing robot has a unique name.

Use the instructions above to complete `robot_name.py`. Keep the existing function and class names: tests you cannot see import them. Use only the Python standard library.

---

{"summary": "I finished `Robot` in `robot_name.py`. Each new robot gets a random name made of two uppercase letters and three digits, and `reset()` gives it a new one.

- **Unique names:** the class keeps a record of every name currently in use, and new names are redrawn until they don't match any of them.
- **Reset:** the new name is chosen while the old one is still marked as taken, so a robot can't get its previous name back, even if the random generator has been re-seeded the same way. After that, the old name is freed for other robots.
- **Limit:** if all 676,000 possible names are in use, creating another robot raises an error.

The project has no test files, so I ran a short inline Python check instead. It confirmed the name format, that a name changes after a reset with a re-seeded generator, and that 5,000 robots all got different names. It printed `ok`. The hidden tests you mentioned haven't been run against it."}
